::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Operators adapted from prior work.** Plexus re-implements published simulation code
as registered operators: attraction–repulsion and boids from
[ParticleGraph](https://github.com/allierc/ParticleGraph); the slime-mould (Physarum)
agent from [Sebastian Lague's Slime-Simulation](https://github.com/SebLague/Slime-Simulation);
softened self-gravity from Philip Mocz's *Create Your Own N-body Simulation* (2020); the
continuum solver from MLS-MPM (Hu et al. 2018); and the strange attractors from their
originating papers (Lorenz 1963, Rössler 1976, Sprott 1994, …).
:::

Living systems are mechanical, chemical, electrical, and developmental at once.
Computational biology has answered each of these with its own simulator — neural
simulators for electrical activity, reaction–diffusion solvers for chemical
transport, particle and continuum methods for mechanics, vertex and Cellular-Potts
models for tissues. These frameworks remain largely incompatible: coupling
signalling, mechanics, metabolism, and development means bolting specialized
simulators together, each carrying its own representation of what a biological
mechanism *is*. The obstacle is not primarily numerical. **It is a language
problem.**

Plexus treats biological *mechanisms* — not simulators — as the primary objects.
Rather than building another simulator, it defines a common language whose central
elements are **biological operators**: adhesion, diffusion, division, chemotaxis,
electrical propagation, active stress. Every operator specifies the entities it
acts on, the state it reads and writes, the relations between those entities, and
one or more numerical implementations. Biological modelling then becomes analogous
to compiler design.

## A typed intermediate representation

Just as a modern compiler separates a programming language from the machine it runs
on through an **intermediate representation**, Plexus separates a biological
mechanism from its numerical realization. An operator is defined by a **typed
signature** — *what* biological transformation it performs — and by one or more
**implementations** — *how* that transformation is computed. The signature is the
biological contract; the implementation is a numerical choice.

`neuron_voltage` is the contract "membrane state → its derivative," which
Hodgkin–Huxley, Izhikevich, a Neural ODE, or an MLP all satisfy interchangeably;
a mechanical interaction is the contract that MLS-MPM, finite elements, a vertex
model, or a phase field all realize. Because a mechanism is stated once,
independently of its solver, models written for different simulators compile to the
*same* operators, and existing simulators become **complementary backends** rather
than competing paradigms — Plexus is to a biophysics simulator what an intermediate
representation is to a compiler.

## Four concepts, seven operators

The language is built from four concepts — **operators**, and the three kinds of
thing they act on: **sets** (discrete biological entities across scales — particles,
cells, neurons, synapses, tissues), the **state** each element carries, and
**fields** (continuous quantities — morphogens, pressure, potentials). A biological
model is a composition of operators over these objects.

The central wager of Plexus is that a large fraction of the existing simulation
literature can be written with a compact algebra of **seven operator families**:

![The elementary operator algebra. The first four move biological *state*: *Lateral* within a set; *Aggregate* and *Broadcast* up and down across containment $\pi$; *Exchange* to and from a field. The last three change structure: *Rewire* the relations between entities, *Divide* and *Die* the entities themselves.](figures/fig_ops.png){width=100% fig-align="center"}

- **Lateral** — interactions within a set (forces, adhesion, signalling).
- **Aggregate ↑** and **Broadcast ↓** — many-to-one and one-to-many transforms
  across biological scales.
- **Exchange** — coupling between sets and continuous fields (secretion, sensing,
  particle–grid transfer).
- **Rewire** — modification of the relations between entities.
- **Divide** and **Die** — creation and removal of entities.

The first four transform biological *state* while preserving organization; Rewire
changes the interaction *graph*; Divide and Die change the *entities* themselves.
The full algebra — typed signatures, the containment graph, stateful edge-sets, the
one-operator-many-implementations rule, and how division stays differentiable — is
on **[The language](language.qmd)**.

## Composing mechanisms

A biological model is an ordered **schedule** of operator applications. One
simulation step is the composition
$\Phi = \mathcal{O}_n \circ \cdots \circ \mathcal{O}_1$, iterated as
$x_{t+1}=\Phi(x_t)$. Operators are *pure*: each returns its contribution $\Delta_i$
and the engine sums them, so introducing a mechanism is adding a line to the
schedule, never editing the engine. A cell that secretes a chemical, climbs it, and
self-aggregates through its constituent particles is a handful of operators:

```yaml
name: aggregate
sets:
  cell: {n: 100, types: {soft: {fraction: 0.5, youngs: 12}, stiff: {fraction: 0.5, youngs: 300}}}
  particle: {parent: cell, per_parent: 100, radius: 0.02}
fields:
  chemical: {frame: grid, res: 96, diffusion: 0.1, decay: 0.05, couples_to: cell}
operators:
  - {op: secrete, at: "cell[type=soft]", to: chemical, rate: 1.0}    # only soft cells make it
  - {op: sense,   at: "cell[type=soft]", from: chemical, gain: 150}  # only soft cells follow it
  - {op: mpm,     at: particle, n_grid: 128, a_max: 800, drag: 4}
schedule: [aggregate, secrete, chemical.diffuse, sense, mpm]
```

The schedule can be *multi-rate*: mechanics may run every tick while diffusion,
growth, or division fire less often. And because nothing is mutated in place,
gradients flow through the sums and the integrator — the whole rollout stays
**differentiable**, so differentiability is a property of the *language*, not of any
one solver.

## What it looks like

Qualitatively different dynamical systems expressed in the same operator language.
Each is built from the same primitives — sets, state, fields, operators, and a
schedule — yet gives rise to distinct collective behaviour: flocking,
self-organizing networks, self-gravity, deterministic chaos.

## Mechanistic inverse modelling

Because every operator carries a differentiable implementation, gradients propagate
through a composition of *explicit* biological mechanisms rather than through opaque
simulator code. This changes what inference means. Classical calibration assumes the
mechanism is already correct and only tunes parameters — effective when the forward
model is complete, but misleading when a mechanism is *missing*, since optimizing the
present parameters merely compensates for the absent one.

In Plexus, parameters stay attached to named operators — stiffness to mechanical
operators, reaction rates to biochemical ones, conductances to signalling ones — so
estimation preserves the mechanistic meaning of the model, and the residual acquires
one too. A persistent mismatch between simulation and experiment is read not only as
poor parameters but as evidence that the current operator composition cannot explain
the data: a **missing operator**.

The same differentiability lets biological designs be *optimized*. Below, a foraging
colony in a maze is tuned by a UCB search — from a hand-set design (left) to the best
found (right), which delivers food roughly five-fold faster.

## Agentic mechanistic discovery

Because mechanisms are explicit operators rather than simulator-specific code, they
are directly accessible to agentic systems — which turns discovery from a parameter
search into a **search over model structures**. Plexus organizes this as three loops,
each at a higher level of abstraction:

- **Loop I — Understanding.** Decompose an existing simulator into Plexus operators,
  recovering an explicit mechanistic description from opaque code.
- **Loop II — Fitting.** Fit the resulting composition to observations through its
  differentiable implementations, preserving the link between parameters and
  mechanisms.
- **Loop III — Discovery.** Read the residual: propose new operators, compare
  competing mechanistic hypotheses, and extend the algebra when existing mechanisms
  fall short.

The language itself becomes the object of discovery — new biological knowledge is a
new operator, not merely a tuned parameter.

## The operator atlas

This defines a research program with three objectives: build an **algebra** of
biological operators; **decompose** the existing corpus of simulation frameworks into
that common language; and construct **differentiable** implementations so mechanistic
models can be inferred from data. The second objective is the **operator atlas** —
existing frameworks (Chaste, CompuCell3D, Morpheus, Tissue Forge, PhysiCell, Jaxley,
BrainPy, connectome GNNs, …) treated not as rival simulators but as repositories of
reusable mechanisms, each decomposed into operators, typed signatures, and
implementations.

The atlas is also the test of the central hypothesis: if decomposing a broad
collection of simulators converges toward a compact, reusable vocabulary, the operator
algebra is a meaningful intermediate representation for biology; if genuinely new
families keep appearing, the language is still incomplete and extends. Either way, the
vocabulary grows monotonically and every earlier model keeps working.
